query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The retention or loss of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the interaction between lattice strain, dislocation behavior, and nano-twinning.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys with a random solid solution and high entropy of mixing.
generation.intervention: Controlled introduction of lattice strain through alloy composition engineering or mechanical deformation.
generation.conditions: Varied temperature and dwell time conditions during spark plasma sintering.
generation.mechanism: The lattice strain causes unusual dislocation behaviors, such as multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips, resulting in strengthening mechanisms that underpin the strength-ductility synergy. Nano-twinning contributes an additional deformation mode that helps alleviate the deleterious effects of high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced mechanical strength and toughness due to the optimized interaction between lattice strain, dislocation behavior, and nano-twinning.
generation.baseline: Conventional high-entropy alloys without controlled introduction of lattice strain or nano-twinning.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis should hold within the boundaries of high-entropy alloys with a random solid solution and high entropy of mixing, and under varied temperature and dwell time conditions during spark plasma sintering.
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between lattice strain, dislocation behavior, and nano-twinning is not fully understood and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: A controlled experiment introducing lattice strain through alloy composition engineering or mechanical deformation, and measuring the resulting dislocation behavior and nano-twinning.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of lattice strain does not result in enhanced mechanical strength and toughness due to optimized dislocation behavior and nano-twinning, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, we realize the design of bioinspired all-ceramics that feature a contiguous network of the Cr7C3 plastic phase uniformly distributed within the predominant HEC [i.e., (Hf, Zr, Ta, Nb, Ti, Cr)C] hard phase, through the high-entropy composition-engineering strategy. Specifically, the resulting HEC/Cr7C3 all-ceramics show high KIC of 12.5 ± 1.5 MPa·m1/2 and flexural strength of 613 ± 52 MPa at room temperature (RT), and good strength retention of ~97% up to 1300 °C, surpassing the performance of most other reported bioinspired ceramics. Further in-situ experimental and theoretical investigations provide compelling evidence that the Cr7C3 phase can plastically deform under load, achieving a ~ 30.8% compression strain through forming nanoscale shear bands with significant crystal defects. This plastic deformation behavior, which does not rely on specific crystallographic orientations, effectively enriches the toughening mechanisms in HEC/Cr7C3 all-ceramics. Our materials are promising in numerous applications e.g., advanced manufacturing, metallurgy, chemical industry, and aerospace, especially at elevated temperatures.

From the images in Fig. 3, the nano-twins in the EBSD scans become very clear by overlaying the scan on an image quality, IQ, map of the same data set, which permits the measurement of the typical misorientation angle of 60° for twinning (Fig. 3e). We conclude from these results that between room and cryogenic temperatures where the strength, ductility and toughness of the medium-entropy CrCoNi are all simultaneously enhanced, nano-twinning contributes an important additional deformation mode that helps alleviate the deleterious effects of high strength that would normally be expected to result in lower toughness.

Our results reveal that the heterogeneous lattice strain causes unusual dislocation behaviors (i.e., multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips), resulting in the strengthening mechanisms that underpin the strength-ductility synergy. The outcome of our research sheds important insights into the design of strong yet ductile distorted crystalline solids, such as high-entropy alloys and high-entropy ceramics.
